sets.title: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. For questions 1–20, find the relevant information. Spelling matters for short answers. Time target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Initial assessment & risk
texts.body:
Acute upper GI bleeding (AUGIB) presents with haematemesis, melaena, or both. Syncope, resting tachycardia, or postural hypotension suggest significant volume loss.

Immediate priorities
• Protect airway if ongoing massive haematemesis or reduced consciousness
• Two large-bore IV cannulae; send FBC, urea/electrolytes, coagulation, group and save (cross-match if unstable)
• Restrictive transfusion threshold usually haemoglobin <70 g/L in otherwise stable patients without cardiovascular ischaemia; higher targets may apply in ischaemic heart disease

Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) — outpatient pathway
A GBS of 0 identifies very-low-risk patients who may be considered for early discharge with urgent outpatient endoscopy rather than admission, provided social support and follow-up are reliable.

Rockall score (post-endoscopy)
Combines age, shock, comorbidity and endoscopic stigmata to estimate rebleeding and mortality risk. Do not use Rockall alone to decide pre-endoscopy triage.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Resuscitation & medical therapy algorithm
texts.body:
Step 1 — ABC and volume
Crystalloid bolus if hypotensive. Avoid over-transfusion in variceal disease (target Hb often ~70–80 g/L) because excess volume may increase portal pressure.

Step 2 — Reverse coagulopathy when indicated
• Stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants after senior discussion; do not reverse aspirin routinely before endoscopy if cardiac stents are recent — involve cardiology
• For warfarin with active major bleed: vitamin K IV + PCC as per local protocol
• DOAC major bleed: specific reversal agents where available; otherwise PCC per haematology advice

Step 3 — Acid suppression & vasoactive drugs
• Non-variceal: high-dose PPI infusion after endoscopic haemostasis (e.g. continuous omeprazole/pantoprazole infusion for 72 hours in high-risk stigmata). Pre-endoscopy PPI may be given but does not replace timely endoscopy.
• Suspected variceal bleed: start terlipressin (or octreotide if terlipressin unavailable) AND prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. IV ceftriaxone) before endoscopy.

Step 4 — Escalate early
Massive transfusion protocol if ongoing instability. Contact gastroenterology and ICU early for unstable patients.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Endoscopy timing & findings checklist
texts.body:
Timing (door-to-endoscopy guidance)
• Immediate (as soon as resuscitated): ongoing haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation, suspected variceal bleed with instability
• Within 24 hours: most admitted AUGIB patients once adequately resuscitated
• Very low risk (GBS 0): may defer to urgent outpatient slot within days if local pathway allows

Pre-endoscopy checklist
• Informed consent / capacity assessment
• NBM status documented; airway risk discussed with anaesthesia if GCS reduced
• Erythromycin IV 30–60 minutes pre-procedure may improve mucosal views in selected cases (local protocol)

High-risk endoscopic stigmata (non-variceal)
Active spurting/oozing, non-bleeding visible vessel, adherent clot — these usually need endoscopic therapy and post-procedure high-dose PPI.

Failure of endoscopic control
Arrange interventional radiology (embolisation) or surgery after joint discussion; do not delay transfer while repeating ineffective endoscopy cycles.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Post-endoscopy care & discharge criteria
texts.body:
Monitoring
• Hourly observations initially if high-risk stigmata treated; step down when stable
• Clear fluid then diet as directed by endoscopist; record any recurrent melaena/haematemesis on fluid chart

Medication plan
• Continue PPI orally after IV course completes, typically 4–8 weeks depending on ulcer pathology and H. pylori status
• Test for H. pylori (biopsy or urea breath/stool antigen when appropriate); treat if positive
• Restart necessary antithrombotics at the earliest safe interval agreed by gastroenterology/cardiology — often within 1–3 days for aspirin after haemostasis, longer for anticoagulants

Discharge only if ALL met
• Haemodynamically stable ≥24 hours after therapy
• Haemoglobin stable on two consecutive checks
• Tolerating oral intake
• Clear safety-net advice given (return if black stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, syncope)
• Follow-up endoscopy booked when indicated (e.g. gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy)

sets.title: Neutropenic sepsis pathway
sets.instruction: Four texts on neutropenic sepsis. Answer questions 1–20 using only the texts.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Definitions & immediate red flags
texts.body:
Neutropenic sepsis is a time-critical emergency. Treat suspected cases before neutrophil count returns if clinical suspicion is high.

Working definitions (adult)
• Neutropenia: absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <1.0 × 10⁹/L (some protocols use <0.5 × 10⁹/L for ‘profound’)
• Fever: single oral temperature ≥38.3°C OR ≥38.0°C sustained for 1 hour
• Suspected neutropenic sepsis: fever OR other signs of infection in a patient at risk (recent chemotherapy, known haematological malignancy, stem-cell transplant) even if ANC not yet available

Red flags requiring immediate escalation
• Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg or drop ≥40 mmHg from baseline)
• Respiratory rate ≥25/min or new oxygen requirement
• Altered mental state
• Rigors with unstable observations
• Suspected source requiring source control (e.g. line infection with septic shock)

Do not wait for laboratory confirmation of neutropenia before giving the first antibiotic dose if the patient is at risk and septic.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Door-to-needle pathway (first hour)
texts.body:
Time targets from arrival / recognition
0–15 minutes
• Alert: ‘neutropenic sepsis pathway’
• ABC assessment; high-flow oxygen if SpO₂ <94% (or target per COPD protocol)
• IV access ×2; blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics whenever this does not delay therapy >15 minutes total

By 60 minutes (door-to-needle)
• First broad-spectrum IV antibiotic administered — commonly piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) as monotherapy if no penicillin allergy; alternatives per local antibiogram (e.g. meropenem if indicated)
• Lactate, FBC, U&E, CRP, clotting, group and save
• Fluid challenge if hypotensive (crystalloid 500 mL rapid bolus, reassess; repeat as needed while arranging critical care review)

Cultures & samples
• Peripheral blood cultures ± paired from central line hubs if line present
• Mid-stream urine if possible; swab any wounds; CXR if respiratory signs
• Do not delay antibiotics for imaging

If penicillin anaphylaxis history
Use locally approved non-penicillin regimen (e.g. ciprofloxacin + vancomycin — only if listed in your trust guideline).

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Risk stratification & ongoing antibiotics
texts.body:
MASCC risk index (selected low-risk outpatient pathways)
Higher MASCC scores indicate lower risk of complications. Only use outpatient oral therapy if ALL of the following apply per local policy: haemodynamically stable, no organ failure, reliable social support, able to tolerate oral medication, and MASCC high (commonly ≥21). Most inpatient oncology pathways still admit for IV therapy initially.

IV catheter / line suspected
• Examine exit site; if tunnel infection or septic shock with likely line source, discuss line removal with oncology/microbiology early
• Add vancomycin (or teicoplanin) when MRSA risk, severe mucositis, or suspected catheter-related infection — follow local dosing/levels

Reassessment at 48 hours
• If cultures negative, afebrile, and recovering neutrophils, consider de-escalation
• Persistently febrile after 72–96 hours: review for fungal infection, occult source, and discuss antifungal strategy with haematology/ID

G-CSF
Not routinely required for every febrile neutropenic episode; consider when profound neutropenia with high-risk features per oncology advice.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Patient information & discharge safety-netting
texts.body:
Education before chemotherapy discharge
Give written advice to present IMMEDIATELY if:
• Temperature ≥38.0°C
• Uncontrolled shivering/rigors
• Flu-like illness, new cough, shortness of breath
• Burning urine, diarrhoea with fever, severe mucositis preventing intake
• Dizziness, confusion, or feeling ‘the worst ever’

Home pack (where commissioned)
Some services provide emergency oral antibiotics to start after phone triage — patients must still attend for assessment the same day unless a formal telemedicine pathway confirms low risk.

After inpatient treatment — discharge criteria
• Afebrile ≥24 hours on appropriate therapy
• Clinically stable; ANC recovering or infection controlled
• Oral route reliable; follow-up bloods/clinic booked
• Clear advice on central-line care if discharged with a line

Documentation must record time of first antibiotic dose (door-to-needle) for audit.

sets.title: Peri-operative anticoagulation bridging

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Who needs bridging? Risk categories
texts.body:
Bridging = temporary use of short-acting anticoagulant (usually LMWH) when a vitamin-K antagonist (VKA) such as warfarin is interrupted for a procedure.

Higher thromboembolic risk (bridging more often considered)
• Mechanical mitral valve OR older-generation mechanical aortic valve
• AF with prior stroke/TIA and CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥5 (local cut-offs vary)
• VTE within the preceding 3 months
• Previous VTE during interruption of anticoagulation

Lower risk (bridging often unnecessary)
• Uncomplicated AF with lower CHA₂DS₂-VASc
• Remote VTE >12 months ago and no thrombophilia
• Bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without other risk factors (many guidelines advise against routine bridging)

DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
Usually stopped for a procedure-specific interval based on renal function and bleeding risk; routine LMWH bridging is NOT recommended for DOACs.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Warfarin interruption timetable
texts.body:
Standard elective procedure (therapeutic INR 2.0–3.0)
• Last warfarin dose: 5 days before procedure (i.e. hold for 5 doses) in most adults
• Check INR the day before surgery; if INR >1.5, consider low-dose oral vitamin K per protocol and recheck
• Target pre-op INR usually ≤1.5 for surgery with bleeding risk (specialty-specific exceptions exist)

High bleeding-risk procedures (examples)
Neuraxial anaesthesia, major cancer surgery, prostate/bladder resection, intracranial/spinal surgery — require longer clean anticoagulant windows and stricter INR targets.

Restart warfarin
• Evening of surgery or day 1 if haemostasis secure, at usual maintenance dose (± bridging overlap until INR therapeutic)
• Do not ‘load’ with large unexpected doses without senior/haematology input

texts.label: C
texts.heading: LMWH bridging doses & holding rules
texts.body:
When bridging is indicated (VKA patients)
• Start therapeutic LMWH when INR falls below therapeutic range (often ~36–48 hours after last warfarin), e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC twice daily OR 1.5 mg/kg once daily (prefer BD in higher-risk; adjust for CrCl <30 mL/min)

Hold LMWH before procedure
• Last therapeutic dose: 24 hours before surgery for twice-daily regimens
• For once-daily therapeutic regimens: give half the dose the morning before surgery, then hold
• Prophylactic-dose LMWH (if used instead of therapeutic bridging): last dose ≥12 hours pre-op

Post-procedure restart
• Prophylactic LMWH ≥12 hours after surgery if haemostasis OK
• Therapeutic LMWH usually delayed 48–72 hours after high bleeding-risk surgery
• Overlap LMWH with warfarin until INR ≥2.0 for two consecutive days (or per valve clinic target)

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Neuraxial anaesthesia & emergency surgery notes
texts.body:
Neuraxial block (spinal/epidural) — minimum intervals after LMWH
• Prophylactic enoxaparin: wait ≥12 hours after last dose before needle placement
• Therapeutic enoxaparin: wait ≥24 hours
• After catheter removal: wait ≥4 hours before next LMWH dose (local anaesthetic protocols may be stricter)

Emergency surgery on warfarin
• Discuss bleeding vs thrombosis risk with surgeon/anaesthetist/haematology
• For immediate reversal: IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (dose by INR/weight per protocol); FFP is second-line if PCC unavailable
• Document indication, products given, and post-reversal INR

Emergency surgery on DOAC
• Record last dose time and renal function
• Delay surgery if safe; if not, consider specific reversal (e.g. idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet where available for factor-Xa inhibitors) or PCC per haematology
